card.title: Work Done by a Constant Force and a Variable Force

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Definition of work (constant force):** $W = F s \\\\cos\ heta$, where $F$ is the magnitude of the constant force, $s$ is the displacement, and $\ heta$ is the angle between the force vector and displacement vector. Work is a scalar quantity - it has magnitude but no direction.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Work is NOT force times distance in general - it is force component in the direction of displacement times distance. $W = F s$ only when force and displacement are parallel ($ heta = 0$).…
Work done BY a force vs work done ON an object: $W_{\ ext{by}} = -W_{\ ext{on}}$. The work-energy theorem uses $W_{\ ext{net}}$ (work done BY all forces ON the object).…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Holding a heavy object stationary: You exert a force, but displacement is zero, so $W = 0$! You get tired because your muscles do internal biochemical work (energy conversion), not mechanical work on the object. This is a classic misconception.  ·  Centripetal force does NO work: $F_c$ is always perpendicular to velocity (displacement), so $\\\\cos 90^\\\\circ = 0$. It changes direction, not speed. A planet in circular orbit around the Sun has zero work done by gravity.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The concept of work was formalized by Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis in 1829. He defined 'work' as the product of force and distance - the word 'work' in physics has a precise mathematical meaning different from everyday usage.  ·  Work is a SCALAR, not a vector. It has no direction, only magnitude and sign. Energy (which work changes) is also a scalar. This is why we can add works from different forces as simple numbers: $W_{\ ext{net}} = W_1 + W_2 + \\\\dots$

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: A 5 kg block is pulled 10 m across a horizontal floor by a force of 20 N at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. Find (a) work done by the applied force, (b) work done by friction, (c) net work, (d) final speed if it started from rest. Solution: (a) $W_F = F s \\\\cos 30^\\\\circ = 20 \ imes 10 \ imes 0.866 = 173.2$ J.…  ·  A force $F(x) = 3x^2 + 2x$ N acts on a particle moving along the x-axis from $x = 1$ m to $x = 3$ m. Find the work done. Solution: $W = \\\\int_1^3 (3x^2 + 2x) dx = [x^3 + x^2]_1^3 = (27 + 9) - (1 + 1) = 36 - 2 = 34$ J.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: For a variable force, you CANNOT just multiply 'average force' by distance unless you know the average is the integral average. The correct method is always integration or graphical area. A common error: averaging endpoints $\ rac{F_i + F_f}{2}$ only works for linear forces.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Sign of work:** Work is POSITIVE when $0^\\\\circ \\\\le \ heta < 90^\\\\circ$ (force component along displacement). Work is ZERO when $\ heta = 90^\\\\circ$ (force perpendicular to displacement, e.g., centripetal force, normal force on horizontal surface). Work is NEGATIVE when $90^\\\\circ < \ heta \\\\le 180^\\\\circ$ (force opposes displacement, e.g., kinetic friction, gravity when lifting).  ·  **Work by multiple forces:** Total work is the sum of works by individual forces: $W_{\ ext{net}} = \\\\sum W_i = \\\\sum F_i s \\\\cos\ heta_i$. This is equivalent to the work done by the net force: $W_{\ ext{net}} = F_{\ ext{net}} s \\\\cos\ heta_{\ ext{net}}$.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: The work-energy theorem $W_{\ ext{net}} = \\\\Delta K$ is mathematically equivalent to Newton's second law $F = ma$. It's not a new law - it's a reformulation that is often easier to use when forces vary or the path is complex.  ·  One joule (1 J) is the work done by a force of 1 newton moving an object 1 meter in the direction of the force. It's a small amount: lifting a 100 g apple by 1 m does about 1 J of work against gravity.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A spring with $k = 200$ N/m is compressed from 0.1 m to 0.3 m. Find (a) work done BY the spring, (b) work done ON the spring by an external agent. Solution: (a) $W_{\ ext{spring}} = \ rac{1}{2}k(x_i^2 - x_f^2) = 100 \ imes (0.01 - 0.09) = -8$ J. Spring does negative work (it pushes back). (b) $W_{\ ext{ext}} = +8$ J.…  ·  A 2 kg block slides down a frictionless incline of length 5 m and angle 30°. Find the work done by gravity and the final speed. Solution: Vertical drop $h = 5 \\\\sin 30^\\\\circ = 2.5$ m. $W_g = mgh = 2 \ imes 9.8 \ imes 2.5 = 49$ J. $W_g = \\\\Delta K = \ rac{1}{2}mv^2 \ ightarrow v = \\\\sqrt{2 \ imes 49 / 2} = 7$ m/s.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: In thermodynamics, work is energy transfer across a system boundary due to macroscopic forces. The same definition $W = \\\\int F dx$ applies, but the 'system' and 'surroundings' must be clearly defined.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Variable force definition:** When force varies with position, work is the integral of force over the displacement: $W = \\\\int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) \\\\, dx$ (for 1D motion). Graphically, this is the area under the $F$ vs $x$ curve between the initial and final positions.  ·  **Work by a spring force (Hooke's law):** For an ideal spring, $F = -kx$. Work done BY the spring when moving from $x_i$ to $x_f$: $W_{\ ext{spring}} = \\\\int_{x_i}^{x_f} (-kx) dx = \ rac{1}{2}k x_i^2 - \ rac{1}{2}k x_f^2$. Work done ON the spring (by external agent) is the negative of this.  ·  **Work by gravity (near Earth):** Gravity is a constant force $F_g = mg$ downward. If an object moves vertically by $\\\\Delta y$ (up positive), $W_g = -mg \\\\Delta y$. If it moves horizontally, $W_g = 0$. For a path with vertical drop $h$, $W_g = +mgh$ (gravity does positive work).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The force on a particle is $F(x) = 10 - 2x$ N. The particle moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 6$ m. Find the work done and explain the physical meaning of the negative work portion. Solution: $W = \\\\int_0^6 (10 - 2x) dx = [10x - x^2]_0^6 = 60 - 36 = 24$ J.…  ·  **Work by a constant force in 2D/3D:** $W = \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot \\\\vec{s} = F_x s_x + F_y s_y + F_z s_z$. Only the component of force parallel to displacement contributes. This dot product form is frame-independent.  ·  **Work-energy connection (preview):** The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\ ext{net}} = \\\\Delta K = \ rac{1}{2}mv_f^2 - \ rac{1}{2}mv_i^2$. This is the work-energy theorem, derived from Newton's second law.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Path dependence for variable forces:** For a variable force, work depends on the path taken. For conservative forces (gravity, spring), work is path-independent and equals $-\\\\Delta U$. For non-conservative forces (friction), work depends on the actual path length.  ·  **Graphical interpretation:** The area under the $F$-$x$ curve (with sign) gives the work. Positive area = positive work; negative area = negative work. For a spring, the $F$-$x$ graph is a straight line through origin with slope $k$, and the area is a triangle $\ rac{1}{2}kx^2$.  ·  **Work by a varying force in 2D:** $W = \\\\int_C \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot d\\\\vec{r} = \\\\int_C (F_x dx + F_y dy)$. This is a line integral. For a force $\\\\vec{F}(x,y)$, the work along path C depends on the specific curve C unless $\\\\vec{F}$ is conservative ($\ abla \ imes \\\\vec{F} = 0$).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Constant force vs variable force summary:** Constant force: $W = F s \\\\cos\ heta$ (simple product). Variable force: $W = \\\\int F(x) dx$ (area under curve). Both are special cases of the general definition $W = \\\\int \\\\vec{F} \\\\cdot d\\\\vec{r}$.  ·  **Example - work by gravity on an incline:** Block slides down incline of angle $\ heta$, length $L$. Vertical drop $h = L \\\\sin\ heta$. Work by gravity: $W_g = mgh = mgL \\\\sin\ heta$. This equals force component parallel to incline ($mg\\\\sin\ heta$) times distance $L$.  ·  **Example - work by external agent stretching a spring:** Slowly stretch spring from 0 to $x$ (quasi-static, acceleration $\\\\approx 0$). Applied force $F_{\ ext{app}} = +kx$ (matches spring force). Work done: $W = \\\\int_0^x kx dx = \ rac{1}{2}kx^2$. This energy is STORED as elastic potential energy in the spring.
